overview:
The term "Nirayavalika group" (often referred to as Nirayāvalikā-ādi Sutratraya) designates a closely related cluster of three Jain Upāṅga scriptures: Nirayāvalikā (also called Kalpika), Kalpāvatāṃsikā, and Puṣpikā. These texts belong to the Angabahya (external) section of the Śvetāmbara Jain Āgama canon and are classified under Dharma-kathānuyoga, the narrative branch of scriptural literature. Together, they present a structured set of didactic stories illustrating the workings of karma, the consequences of violence and attachment, and the path of renunciation and liberation.

Within the broader Āgama system, the Nirayāvalika group is traditionally associated as subsidiary (Upāṅga) material to the Antakṛt-daśā (Antagaḍa) Sūtra. The group is organized to show a progression of karmic destinies: beings falling into hellish realms (niraya), beings reborn in celestial realms (devaloka), and beings connected with special spiritual states or auspicious circumstances. By narrating the lives of princes, queens, and dynasties—especially those linked to King Śreṇika of Rājagṛha and his son Kūṇika (Ajātaśatru)—the texts embed doctrinal teaching in vivid historical and semi-legendary episodes.

The Nirayāvalikā itself focuses on the destinies of ten princes (kumāras) and their mothers, many of whom are related to King Śreṇika. Their stories show how cruelty, ambition, and war lead to suffering and hellish rebirth, while remorse, right faith, and renunciation open the way to liberation. Kalpāvatāṃsikā shifts attention to heavenly rebirths and the conditions that lead to residence in various celestial regions, emphasizing that even devaloka is impermanent and inferior to mokṣa. Puṣpikā further elaborates on beings connected with celestial phenomena and particular spiritual states, reinforcing the message that all conditioned existence—whether hellish, human, or heavenly—is governed by karma and is ultimately transient.

As a group, these three Upāṅgas are important for understanding how Jain tradition uses narrative to convey complex doctrinal themes. They illustrate the law of karma, the dangers of political power and violence, and the transformative potential of contact with Tīrthaṅkaras and their disciples. At the same time, the Nirayāvalika group preserves valuable historical and cultural memory about Magadha, Vaiśālī, the Mahāśilākaṇṭaka war, and the social milieu around Lord Mahāvīra. Modern editions and translations—often accompanied by extensive commentaries—continue to be studied in Śvetāmbara communities, especially among Sthānakavāsī and Mūrtipūjaka traditions, as narrative complements to more doctrinally technical texts.

primary_sources.title: Nirayāvalikā Sūtra (Nirayavalika, Kalpika)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the canonical transmission of Sudharmāsvāmin; preserved in Śvetāmbara Āgama tradition
primary_sources.original_text: णिरयावलिआए कालो सुकालो महाकालो कृष्णो सुकृष्णो महाकृष्णो वीरकृष्णो रामकृष्णो पितुसेणकृष्णो महासेणकृष्णो तेसिं णामे णिरयावलिकाए अद्धयणाए।
primary_sources.transliteration: Nirayāvalikāe kālo sukālo mahākālo kṛṣṇo sukṛṣṇo mahākṛṣṇo vīrakṛṣṇo rāmakṛṣṇo pituseṇakṛṣṇo mahāseṇakṛṣṇo tesiṃ nāme nirayāvalikāe adhyayaṇāe.
primary_sources.translation: In the Nirayāvalikā there are the studies named Kāl, Sukāl, Mahākāl, Kṛṣṇa, Sukṛṣṇa, Mahākṛṣṇa, Vīrakṛṣṇa, Rāmakṛṣṇa, Pituseṇakṛṣṇa, and Mahāseṇakṛṣṇa.
primary_sources.notes: This passage, cited in traditional Prakrit form, summarizes the ten adhyayanas (studies) of the Nirayāvalikā Sūtra. The text is structured as one śrutaskandha with multiple adhyayanas, each narrating the life and karmic destiny of a particular prince. Modern editions (e.g., Sanskrit–Prakrit with Hindi or Gujarati commentaries) emphasize that the Nirayāvalikā is the eighth Upāṅga (Agam 19 in some numbering) and belongs to Dharma-kathānuyoga. The stories of King Śreṇika, Queen Cellaṇā, Kūṇika, and the Mahāśilākaṇṭaka war are central narrative units used to illustrate karmic causality and the dangers of violence and political ambition.

primary_sources.title: Kalpāvatāṃsikā Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara tradition; specific redactor not individually named
primary_sources.original_text: कल्पावतंसिकाए देवलोए भगवतो महावीरस्स उपदेशो देवानं भावो तेसिं उपपत्ति-विहाणं वण्णइ।
primary_sources.transliteration: Kalpāvatamsikāe devaloe bhagavato Mahāvīrassa upadeso devāṇaṃ bhāvo tesiṃ upapatti-vihāṇaṃ vaṇṇai.
primary_sources.translation: In the Kalpāvatāṃsikā, in the celestial realms, the teaching of Lord Mahāvīra describes the states of the gods and narrates the manner of their rebirth.
primary_sources.notes: Kalpāvatāṃsikā is traditionally counted as the second text in the Nirayāvalika group. It focuses on devaloka (heavenly realms), explaining the karmic causes of celestial rebirth and the limitations of heavenly existence. The text is often studied together with Nirayāvalikā and Puṣpikā in commentarial works such as "Nirayavalika Aadi Sutratray". While the exact wording of early manuscripts varies, the thematic emphasis on Mahāvīra’s discourse to ascetics and the description of various heavens is consistent across editions.

primary_sources.title: Puṣpikā Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara tradition; specific redactor not individually named
primary_sources.original_text: पुस्सपिकाए पुस्सपिकाणं भावो उवसग्गा-देवाणं च विहाणं वण्णइ।
primary_sources.transliteration: Pusspikāe pusspikāṇaṃ bhāvo uvasaggā-devāṇaṃ ca vihāṇaṃ vaṇṇai.
primary_sources.translation: In the Puṣpikā, the states of the Puṣpikā beings and the dwelling of certain calamity-related gods are described.
primary_sources.notes: Puṣpikā is the third text commonly grouped with Nirayāvalikā and Kalpāvatāṃsikā. It elaborates on particular classes of celestial beings and special spiritual or cosmological conditions. The exact classification of these beings differs slightly among commentaries, but the overarching purpose is to show that even extraordinary or auspicious states remain within saṃsāra and are governed by karma. Traditional commentaries stress that the three texts together form a narrative arc: from hellish destinies (Nirayāvalikā) through heavenly rebirths (Kalpāvatāṃsikā) to more nuanced celestial and spiritual states (Puṣpikā), all subordinated to the ultimate goal of mokṣa.

misconceptions.myth: The Nirayāvalika group is only about hell and punishment, with no positive or liberative teachings.
misconceptions.reality: While the Nirayāvalikā Sūtra itself focuses strongly on hellish destinies and the tragic consequences of violence and ambition, the group as a whole (Nirayāvalikā, Kalpāvatāṃsikā, and Puṣpikā) presents a full spectrum of karmic outcomes, including heavenly rebirths and special spiritual states. Many narratives culminate in remorse, renunciation, and liberation, showing that even those deeply entangled in saṃsāra can turn toward right faith and mokṣa.

misconceptions.myth: The stories in the Nirayāvalika group are purely historical chronicles of Magadha and Vaiśālī.
misconceptions.reality: The texts do preserve important historical and cultural memories—such as references to King Śreṇika, Kūṇika (Ajātaśatru), and the Mahāśilākaṇṭaka war—but they are primarily didactic narratives shaped to illustrate Jain doctrines of karma, nonviolence, and renunciation. Their authority in the tradition lies not in providing exact political history but in conveying ethical and spiritual lessons through historically resonant stories.

misconceptions.myth: Because the Nirayāvalika group belongs to the Angabahya section, it is secondary and not important for serious Jain study.
misconceptions.reality: Although classified as Angabahya (external to the core Aṅgas), the Upāṅgas—including the Nirayāvalika group—are integral parts of the Śvetāmbara canon. They are frequently cited in traditional commentaries and modern scholarship for their narrative richness and doctrinal clarity. For understanding Jain views on karma, rebirth, and the socio-political context of Mahāvīra’s era, the Nirayāvalika group is considered highly valuable and is regularly studied alongside more technical doctrinal texts.
